title: Hierarchical geo steering with latency buckets and progressive capacity shedding
creator: Aisha Kumar
description:
Problem: We need a routing policy that preserves low-latency locality while gracefully degrading when regional capacity is constrained. Past incidents showed binary failovers that cause large latency spikes for a subset of customers. Goal: implement a hierarchical geo steering strategy that uses latency buckets, soft geo-pinning, and capacity-aware weights to steer requests. The policy must integrate with existing circuit breakers and load-shedding mechanisms and expose clear telemetry for SLO ownership teams.

Proposed approach:
1) Hierarchy: prefer local region -> prefer nearby peers -> global pool. Each level has configurable soft-pin window (default 5m) before full evacuation.
2) Latency buckets: requests are classified by recent p95/per-route latency into buckets (FAST: <50ms, TRANSIT: 50-150ms, SLOW: >150ms). Routing decisions use the bucket for routing preference: FAST stays local; TRANSIT allows remote peers if local capacity < threshold; SLOW is routed to any available low-cost pool.
3) Capacity hints: each region publishes a rolling capacity score (0-1) derived from GPU availability, queue depth, and cpu headroom. Scores are weighted with SLOs to compute routing weight.
4) Circuit breakers: per-region breakers trigger on combinations of increasing p99 latency, error spikes, and high queue depth. Breakers are soft (reduced weight) before hard open; this allows partial routing away while preserving traffic for graceful degradation.
5) Progressive shedding: when global demand > sustained capacity, we apply graded shedding fractions by priority class. Shedding order: low-priority interactive previews -> batch background -> high-priority live sessions. Shedding uses per-token probabilistic drop, with higher drop rates for lower priority.
6) Fallback model variants: when shedding or capacity constraints detected, requests can be routed to lighter quantized model variants or cached prefix results as configured per-service.
7) Telemetry: expose per-route metrics: routed_fraction_per_region, latency_bucket_histogram, regional_capacity_score, breaker_state, shed_rate_by_priority. Dashboards & SLO alerts will reference these metrics.

Trade-offs and decisions: we chose soft-pin + latency buckets over strict geo pinning to avoid tail amplification in partial outages. Progressive shedding is prioritized by product-defined priority labels to avoid killing high-value sessions. Complexity increases in policy and rollout but yields finer-grained control and smoother degradation.

Rollout plan: implement policy in steering service, unit tests + integration tests, internal canary (10% of requests for 48h), extend to 50% with auto rollback on SLO regression > 5% of baseline. Full rollout after 2 successful cycles and chaos testing.

Open questions:
- Exact latency bucket thresholds and decay windows (proposal uses 50/150ms, open to tuning).
- Failure semantics for stateful sessions (sticky sessions should prefer preserving region).
- How to expose per-customer cost tradeoffs (allow customers to opt into global fallback).
acceptance_criteria: Steering service implements hierarchical policy with configurable levels and soft-pin windows
Latency bucket classifier implemented and used by routing logic
Region capacity score computed and published to the routing mesh
Circuit breaker soft/hard transitions wired to steering weights
Progressive shedding integrated with per-priority labels and can be configured per-service
End-to-end tests simulate region outage and show smooth traffic migration (no >3x p95 increase for >20% of users)
Dashboards show routed_fraction_per_region, breaker_state, capacity_score; alerts configured for SLO regressions
Canary rollout plan executed with rollback criteria and post-canary incident review
